content.content:
\seclabel{revival-inference}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \chapref{type-inference}; \secref{ranges};
\secref{basic-integers}; \secref{revival-ranges}; \secref{revival-notrevised}.
\item[Change] \chapref{type-inference}, which held a heading and two draft
notes, states how the static arguments of a call that does not write them are
inferred, for type parameters and for \KWD{nat} and \KWD{int} parameters.
The declaration is chosen first, as \secref{resolving-coercion} chooses it, a
declaration with static parameters being applicable to a call if some instance
of it within its bounds is, and compared on the parameter types it declares.
Its static arguments are then inferred: a type, \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int}
parameter that a parameter type mentions inside another type is fixed by the
argument, and a type parameter that the return type mentions inside another
type by the expected type; a type parameter that
is the whole type of parameters takes the narrowest type that their arguments
are substitutable for, which for number arguments is the narrowest type into
which every one of them converts, and otherwise, since 29~September 2026, its
bound (below); every
argument is admitted by substitutability, the coercions the instance needs are
inserted statically, and the converted call dispatches by subtyping.
A call written by tight juxtaposition, as a method invocation or as an operator
application, has an expected type in the contexts the chapter lists, a variable
or field declaration and an assignment to a variable among them, and is
inferred again without it when its result then converts.
A numeral whose conversions tie is read as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} by its value; any other tie among
declarations applicable only with coercion is a static error.
The chapter lists what it does not yet describe, the static arguments of a
\KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim}, \KWD{unit} or operator parameter among them, keeps the
second of the two draft notes, and has three boxes: on the Working Draft, the
bound it assumes and the passages it leaves to the revision of the overloading
chapters; on the interpreter; and on a type parameter that only the return
type mentions and on the \KWD{bool} parameters that neither implementation
infers.
The ranges section says that a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a
component converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as an integer numeral does, with a
box.
The box in \secref{basic-integers} says that a generic call over two different
integer types infers the narrowest type that both coerce into by the rule of
\chapref{type-inference}.
\secref{revival-notrevised} says that the rule is written and names the passages
the chapter leaves unrevised, and it and the effect of \secref{revival-ranges}
say that the question of a \KWD{nat} parameter in a range is settled.
On 29~September 2026 one sentence of the rule changed.
Of a type parameter that is the whole type of parameters, where no narrowest
candidate exists and the rule for numerals does not settle the tie, the
chapter said that it ``takes the union of the types of those arguments
(\secref{internal-types}), if its bounds permit that, and none of those
arguments is converted''; it now takes the intersection of its upper bounds,
its declared bound, \TYP{Any} if it has none, and what the expected type
requires of the declared return type, none of those arguments converted, with
a box.
With the revision of the overloading chapters (\secref{revival-overloading}),
the first box points to this entry's list of the cases in which the compiled
type checker departs from the chapter and no longer names the passages that revision revised, and the box
on the interpreter says to which type the interpreter binds such a type
parameter.
A later revision adds an item to the rule: a type parameter that neither an
argument nor the expected type fixes, such as one that only the return type
mentions, as its whole type, likewise takes the intersection of its upper
bounds, and inference never instantiates a static parameter at
\TYP{BottomType}, with an example and a box.
The list of what the chapter does not yet describe named instead ``a static
parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes, such as a type
parameter that only the return type mentions, as its whole type, or the element
type of a reduction that only its generator clauses determine'', and left open
``whether inference may give such a parameter \TYP{BottomType}''; it now names
a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter that nothing fixes, and the element type of
a reduction that only its generator clauses determine, to which the rule gives
the bound of the big operator's static parameter.
The box after the list said that the compiled type checker binds such a type
parameter to \TYP{BottomType}, except that it refuses a call with no expected
type when the parameter is declared \EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Any}}, and that
``whether inference may do so is the team's question, kept in the draft note
below''; it now says that the checker follows the rule, what the compiled path's
bound \TYP{Object} makes of it, what reaches a reduction's big operator and what
the interpreter does, and that the rule answers the third item of the team's
draft note, which the chapter keeps.
A later revision of the interpreter changes both boxes on it.
The box in \secref{static-arg-inference} said that, where no argument's type is
the narrowest, the interpreter ``binds a type parameter that is the whole type
of parameters to the narrowest named common supertype of the arguments'
run-time types that the bounds permit'', the bound only where the bound is that
supertype; it now says that the interpreter gives such a type parameter its
bound, \TYP{Any} if it has none, and does the same where the arguments that fix
a type parameter inside other types have several minimal common supertypes,
except a type parameter whose bound mentions a static parameter and one
declared with several bounds that the interpreter cannot meet, which it binds as
before to the narrowest named common supertype of the arguments' run-time
types, a call that fixes one of the second kind failing where there is none;
that when it chooses among declarations it passes over a declaration with
static parameters whose arguments have several minimal common supertypes in
favour of another applicable without coercion; and that it instantiates at
\TYP{BottomType} a type parameter that an argument bounds only from above.
The box after the list said that ``The interpreter erases a type parameter that
nothing at a call fixes, of a function, to \TYP{BottomType}''; it now says that
the interpreter instantiates such a type parameter at its bound, and one whose
bound mentions other static parameters at that bound with their instances,
except a type parameter that only the bound of a type parameter that the
arguments fix mentions, which it instantiates at the arguments' type, and
names the type parameters it still erases: one declared with several bounds
that it cannot meet, one whose bound mentions the type parameter itself, a big
operator's that a reduction or a comprehension does not write, and one that
only the result of a function expression without a declared return type
fixes.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A.
The revival decided on 26~September 2026 that a generic call over two different
integer types infers the narrowest type that both coerce into, by a rule
written into this chapter; on 27~September 2026 that the compiled type checker
infers static arguments with coercion and keeps the expected type at a call
written as \EXP{f(x)}, with a retry without it so that a coercion of the result
still applies, and that the chapter is written with it; and on 28~September
2026 that a coercion makes a call possible and never changes which declaration
runs when one is applicable without it, the declaration chosen being then
instantiated by that rule, that a numeral whose conversions tie is read as a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and that a \KWD{nat} parameter used as a value converts to
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as a numeral does.
\chapref{multiple-dispatch}, \secref{idn-ref} and \secref{dotted-method-calls}
said that static arguments are inferred as \chapref{type-inference} describes,
and it described nothing; once the compiled type checker infers them by a rule
the text does not state, the text and the implementation disagree, so the
chapter states the rule the checker was built to, and the effect below lists
where the checker departs from it.
The bound in place of the union is the rule by which the dispatcher of the type
group's paper of 2019 instantiates a type parameter that the arguments do not
fix, the intersection of its upper bounds, never \TYP{BottomType}; the team
had assumed the union of the lower bounds, of which the authors write ``we were
unable to complete the proofs of correctness'' (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu,
``Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance'', POPL 2019,
Section~5.4).
The paper gives no algorithm for static inference and asks of it only that it
never instantiate at \TYP{BottomType}; its one example of a static call is
typed at the union of its arguments' types.
The revival decided on 29~September 2026 to take the paper's rule for static
inference as well, which the paper allows and does not require.
The same rule gives a type parameter that neither an argument nor the expected
type fixes the intersection of its upper bounds: the paper's solving step
``never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom'' (Section~5.2), which
answers the question the Working Draft's own note asks, whether type inference
may infer \TYP{BottomType} for a static parameter.
The reasoning for that item, and for the order in which the compiled type
checker tries a call, is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-instance-bound/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.
The revival's decision of 29~September 2026 provided that the interpreter
follow the same rule where it instantiates a declaration, from the run-time
types of the arguments; it has no static return type to add to the bound.
It departs from the rule for the type parameters that the two boxes name,
four kinds by decision and the others as defects.
By decision, a type parameter whose bound mentions the type parameter itself
keeps \TYP{BottomType}: it has no bound to take before its own instance is
known, the paper's calculus admits no type parameter of a method in an upper
bound (p.~11:11), and the revival has not yet decided that case.
By decision, so does a big operator's static parameter that a reduction or a
comprehension does not write: it is the element type of the reduction, which
this chapter does not yet describe, and from \TYP{BottomType} the interpreter's
library builds a comprehension's collection at the type of its elements, where
from the bound it would build it at the bound.
By decision, a type parameter that only the bound of a type parameter that the
arguments fix mentions takes the arguments' type: the interpreter has no
expected type to fix it, and the library's operator that appends two covariant
collections builds its result at such a type parameter, which at its bound
would be \TYP{Any}.
By decision, a lone type parameter whose bound mentions a static parameter,
itself or another, keeps the narrowest named common supertype of the arguments
rather than its bound: the interpreter cannot evaluate such a bound before the
instances are known, and keeping the candidates it had leaves unchanged the
case of a type parameter whose bound mentions itself, which the revival has
not yet decided.
As defects, each gated by an expected failure of the revival's tests, the
interpreter erases to \TYP{BottomType} a type parameter declared with several
bounds that it cannot meet, having no intersection type, a type parameter that
only the result of a function expression without a declared return type fixes,
since it gives that result the type \TYP{BottomType}, and a type parameter that
an argument bounds only from above, since it takes the lower end of the
interval that the arguments give the type parameter.
The reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-walk-instance/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.

content.content:
The order, a declaration chosen and then instantiated, is that of
\secref{resolving-coercion}, read on the parameter types that declarations
declare, as the type group's paper of 2011 reads a declaration with static
parameters: it ``is applicable to a type if and only if at least one of its
instances is'' (\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/setup.tick}, lines 396--397, in the
revival's repository).
The numeral's default is what the interpreter did before this change, giving
a numeral the narrowest of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} that holds its value, \library\ declaring their numeral type
below \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}; the compiled path, whose library declares its
numeral type beside \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and excluding it, took one of the
declarations that a numeral left tied, and not always the same one (row~391 of
the revival's gap ledger).
It is also the Java programming language's type for an integer literal.
The compiled type checker gives a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a
value the type of a numeral, and the interpreter makes it a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
so an \KWD{int} parameter is read as a \KWD{nat} parameter is; on the Java
Virtual Machine the length and the indices of an array are 32-bit integers.
The team's later Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) gives the coercion relation,
the coercion of a generic type and the valid instantiations of a quantified
type (\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines
938--947, 393--400 and 771--789, in the revival's repository) and never uses
the word ``infer''; the type group's paper leaves the run-time inference of the
static arguments of a dispatched declaration ``beyond the scope of this paper''
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/rules.tick}, lines 118--129).
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-inference/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.
\item[Effect] A generic call over two different integer types, or over a number
type and a numeral, need not write its static argument, and the interim rule
of the effect of \secref{revival-numbers} ends.
A declared type fixes a type parameter that the return type of a call written
as \EXP{f(x)} mentions inside another type, and a call whose result the
declared type converts is accepted as before.
Where the conversions of a numeral tie, the \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} declaration or
instance is taken; where another argument's conversions tie, the call is a
static error.
A \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter may be a component of a range, as in the
specification's own examples.
The overloading chapters compare declarations on the parameter types they
declare and infer static arguments after the selection, and \secref{type-param}
gives a type parameter without an \KWD{extends} clause the bound \TYP{Any}
(\secref{revival-overloading}, \secref{revival-bound}).
A type parameter that nothing at a call fixes is instantiated at its bound
under the expected type and never at \TYP{BottomType}: a call whose compiled
run failed loading an instance over \TYP{BottomType}, or failed verification
where the call's result was carried as one, now runs; a call with no expected
type whose type parameter is declared \EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Any}} is
accepted; and a call where the bound and the expected type have no common
subtype, such as a type parameter bounded by \TYP{Object} where \TYP{()} is
expected, is a static error unless the result of the instance at the bound
converts to the expected type.
The compiled type checker departed from the chapter in five cases, each gated
by an expected failure of its tests, until it was revised with the item above:
the expected type could let a declaration applicable only with coercion be
chosen over a declaration with static parameters that is applicable without it
(row~508 of the revival's gap ledger); a call that the rule instantiates at the
bound, with another argument converted, was refused (row~515); a type parameter
declared without an \KWD{extends} clause, which has no narrowest candidate, was
instantiated at the union of the arguments' types where the chapter gives
\TYP{Any} (row~516); an argument that is an instance at a union, which only the
checker's own union made, was refused where it fixes a type parameter
(row~518); and an argument whose static type is an intersection, which the
typing of a call between two traits with \KWD{comprises} clauses gives
(\secref{revival-meet}), fixed a type parameter at one of its conjuncts
(row~541).
It now follows the chapter in each, trying a call by subtyping without the
expected type first and keeping that attempt when its result converts to the
expected type, and the five tests are plain tests of the rule.
The compiled path's run time does not yet load an instance at an intersection
type (row~559), which the rule gives by two routes: an argument whose static
type is an intersection, as in the last of them, and a type parameter that
nothing at a call fixes whose declared bound and expected type are two traits
that meet at their intersection.
A program that the compiled path ran before this revision, at one conjunct of
such an intersection or at \TYP{BottomType}, now dies loading that instance.
A written bound, such as \TYP{Number}, is taken by both implementations where
the chapter gives it.
Under the interpreter, a type parameter that nothing at a call fixes runs at its
bound where it ran at \TYP{BottomType}, and a type parameter with no narrowest
candidate at its bound where it ran at the arguments' narrowest named common
supertype, except the type parameters that the boxes on the interpreter name;
a call whose arguments have several minimal common supertypes runs where it
stopped the interpreter, unless they fix a type parameter declared with several
bounds that the interpreter cannot meet or one whose bound mentions the type
parameter itself.

component AssertRung4
export Executable

(*) Rung 4 of the compile-path ladder: the comparing forms of assert and deny.
(*) The interpreter declares assert(x:Any, y:Any, failMsg:Any...) and the
(*) matching deny at Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:234 and :236 (implementation
(*) Library/FortressLibrary.fss:296 and :306).  The compiler world declares
(*) only assert(Boolean) and assert(Boolean, String) at
(*) Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi:35-36; the comparing form sits commented out at
(*) Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:89-95, so every compilation that writes
(*) assert(x, y) or assert(x, y, msg) stops at typecheck with
(*) "Could not check call to function assert".
(*)
(*) The shapes exercised here are the shapes the blocked programs call, read
(*) off explorations/compile-ladder/raw/tests/: (ZZ32, ZZ32) with an IntLiteral
(*) on either side, (ZZ32, ZZ32, String), (String, String),
(*) (String, String, String) and (Character, Character, String), plus deny at
(*) the same shapes that need the negative direction.
(*)
(*) The vararg form assert(x, y, failMsg: Any...) is deliberately not exercised
(*) and not declared: a vararg parameter does not typecheck against a call whose
(*) arguments need a coercion, so the four programs that write
(*) assert(3, o.foo(), "msg ", o.foo(), " instead of 3.") stay blocked and are
(*) a later rung.
(*)
(*) Both directions are pinned.  Every assert here is given equal arguments and
(*) every deny unequal ones, so a run that prints PASS shows the comparison was
(*) made and came out right; the values are freshly computed rather than
(*) written twice, so an identity comparison on boxed values would not pass.

component FieldBesideInheritedGetter

trait Sized
    getter size(): ZZ32

object Box(size: ZZ32) extends Sized
    twice(): ZZ32 = size + size

content.content:
\section{Applicability for Functionals with Varargs and Keyword Parameters}
\seclabel{applicability-with-special-params}

The basic idea for handling varargs and keyword
parameters is that we
can think of a functional declaration that has such parameters as
though it were (possibly infinitely) many declarations, one for each
set of arguments it may be called with.  In other words, we expand
these declarations so that there exists a declaration for each number
of arguments that can be passed to it.


A declaration with a varargs parameter corresponds to an infinite
number of declarations, one for every number of arguments that may be
passed to the varargs parameter.  In practice, we can bound that
number by the maximum number of arguments that the functional is
called with anywhere in the program (in other words, a given program
will contain only a finite number of calls with different numbers of
arguments).  The expansion described here is a conceptual one to
simplify the description of the semantics; we do not expect a real
implementation to actually expand these declarations at compile time.
%
For example, the following declaration:
%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ, z : ZZ...):ZZ
\begin{Fortress}
\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}\ldots)\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)
\end{Fortress}
would be expanded into:
%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ):ZZ
%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ, z1 : ZZ):ZZ
%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ, z1 : ZZ, z2 : ZZ):ZZ
%f(x : ZZ, y : ZZ, z1 : ZZ, z2 : ZZ, z3 : ZZ):ZZ
%...
\begin{Fortress}
\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{1} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{1} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{2} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
\(f(x \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, y \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{1} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{2} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z}, z_{3} \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Z})\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}\)\\
\(\ldots\)
\end{Fortress}
A declaration with a varargs parameter is applicable to a call if
any one of the expanded declarations is applicable.



\section{Overloading Resolution}
\seclabel{resolving-overloading}
applicable to every call to which $d_1$ is applicable, and not the other way
round (\secref{resolving-overloading}); where neither has static parameters,
this is the relation $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$ of the rules above.
A set of overloaded declarations, some or all of which have static parameters,
is a valid overloading when every pair $d_1$, $d_2$ of them satisfies the
following three rules:
\begin{itemize}
\item
The \emph{No Duplicates Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each more specific than
the other.
\item
The \emph{Meet Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ exclude each other, or one of them is more
specific than the other, or some declaration of the set is more specific than
both and applicable to every call to which both are applicable.
\item
The \emph{Return Type Rule}: if $d_1$ is more specific than $d_2$, then for
every argument type other than \TYP{BottomType} to which $d_1$ is applicable,
and for every instance of $d_2$ that is applicable to it, some instance of $d_1$
is applicable to it whose return type is a subtype of the return type of that
instance of $d_2$.
\end{itemize}

+++ b/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/TypeHierarchyChecker.scala
@@ -27,2 +27,3 @@ import com.sun.fortress.exceptions.TypeError
 import com.sun.fortress.nodes._
+import com.sun.fortress.nodes_util.NodeFactory

@@ -60,2 +61,3 @@ class TypeHierarchyChecker(compilation_unit: CompilationUnitIndex,

     toJavaList(removeDuplicates(toListFromImmutable(errors)))
@@ -63,2 +65,38 @@ class TypeHierarchyChecker(compilation_unit: CompilationUnitIndex,
 
+  /* An object expression that extends a trait with a comprises clause, explicitly or
+   * through the traits it extends, must be a subtype of a listed type, as the trait's
+   * extenders together must be: an object expression has no static parameters and no
+   * comprises clause of its own, and the trait table does not know it. */
+  private def checkObjectExprComprises(ast: Node,
+                                       errors: JavaList[StaticError],
+                                       analyzer: TypeAnalyzer): Unit = {
+    object finder extends Walker {
+      var scope = analyzer
+      private def within(sparams: JavaList[StaticParam], node: Any): Any = {
+        val outer = scope
+        scope = scope.extend(toListFromImmutable(sparams), None)
+        super.walk(node)
+        scope = outer
+        node
+      }
+      override def walk(node: Any): Any = node match {
+        case d: TraitObjectDecl => within(NodeUtil.getStaticParams(d), node)
+        case f: FnDecl => within(NodeUtil.getStaticParams(f), node)
+        case o: ObjectExpr =>
+          val extended = toListFromImmutable(o.getHeader.getExtendsClause).map(_.getBaseType).collect {
+            case t: TraitType => t }
+          val self = NodeFactory.makeMaybeIntersectionType(toJavaList(extended))
+          val closed = (extended ++ extended.flatMap(t => scope.ancestors(t).collect { case a: TraitType => a })).distinct
+          for (t <- closed; listed <- scope.comprisedTypes(t))
+            if (!comprisesContains(listed.map(_.asInstanceOf[NamedType]).toSet, self, scope))
+              error(errors, "Invalid comprises clause: " + t.getName +
+                    " has a comprises clause\n    but an object expression that extends it" +
+                    " is not a subtype of a type it lists.", o)
+          super.walk(node)
+        case _ => super.walk(node)
+      }
+    }
+    finder(ast)
+  }

content.content:
\section{Changes Made by the 2026 Revival to the Working Draft}
\seclabel{revival-changes}
\sloppy

This section lists the changes made to this working draft by the 2026
revival of the Fortress project (\url{https://github.com/palimondo/fortress}).
The revival works to finish what the designers intended, judged by this
working draft, and changes the text only where a decision it has taken for
the implementation would otherwise leave the text and the implementation in
open disagreement.
Each changed passage carries a box headed
``Revised by the 2026 revival'' that points to its entry here.

Each entry gives the affected sections, the change, its rationale, its
effect, the original text, and what reversing to the alternative not taken
would require.
The original text is that of the \emph{Working Draft of February 2011},
the unrevised copy of this document kept in the revival's repository under
the directory \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/}, cited by path and line
there.
The directory's name is misleading: its sources are the working draft of
2~February 2011, and only the file \nolinkurl{fortress.1.0.pdf} in it is the
Fortress~1.0 release.
The full reasoning behind every entry, with each original passage and each
new one, is in the revival's decision records,
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md}
and, for the number chapters,
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-numbers/decision-record.md},
in the same repository.

Each change below follows a decision of the revival.
The first of those decisions, taken on
24~September 2026 and called \emph{route~A}, is that the compiled type checker keeps
the type group's rule that no type is a subtype of two different
instantiations of one parameterized trait, a rule this working draft never
stated, and that the library's numeric types are reorganized so that they
satisfy it.
An entry whose change does not follow from route~A says so, and names the
decision it follows or gives its reason.
The revision of the number chapters (\secref{revival-numbers} to
\secref{revival-reductions}) also carries out three decisions of
26~September 2026 that follow from route~A: on the refined number types, on
conversions between number types, and on sums and products.
The alternative not taken, \emph{route~C}, is described once, in
\secref{revival-routec}.

\subsection{The type of an integer numeral}
\seclabel{revival-numeral-type}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{literals}; \secref{coercion}.
\item[Change] \secref{literals} says that \library\ give every numeral without a
radix point the type \TYP{IntLiteral}, which extends \TYP{Number} and none of the
number types, and that each of the five integer types, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} declares a coercion from it.
The box of \secref{coercion} says the same of the coercion into
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, and that the interpreter does not yet give a numeral that
type.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
on 29~September 2026 that a numeral has a type of its own, \TYP{IntLiteral},
from which each number type converts, the compiled path's own library's working
version taken in place of the numeral types of \secref{literals}, which no
library declares, and that \library\ take it before the interpreter does, since
the interpreter can give a numeral that type without changing the declarations
its calls reach only once it runs with the static types of the compiled type
checker.
\Library\ declared their numeral type an object extending \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
its arithmetic withheld by the comment ``Do not enable these until coercion is
implemented; doing so will cause all our arithmetic to occur on IntLiterals.''
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss}, lines
495--496 before this change, in the revival's repository).
Coercion is implemented on both paths now, and \library\ declare the type as
the compiled path's own library does
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi}, lines
390--431): beside the number types under \TYP{Number}, with the arithmetic that
comment withheld, each integer type declaring a coercion from it.
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, which that library does not declare from
a numeral, coerce from it too, since \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} coerces from every integer
type (\secref{basic-rationals}) and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} from integer numerals
(\secref{revival-int-float}).
\item[Effect] The compiled type checker converts an integer numeral to the
integer type, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} or \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} that its context expects,
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} among them, which refused a numeral
before.
A numeral beside a value of an integer type is converted to that type where no
declaration of the operator is applicable to the two without coercion, and that
type's own declaration of the operator is then the most specific
(\secref{resolving-coercion}); \library\ state on each integer type the
comparisons \EXP{<}, \EXP{\leq}, \EXP{>} and \EXP{\geq}, \OPR{CMP},
\OPR{MAXNUM}, \OPR{MINNUM} and a power with a numeral exponent, which the types
inherited before from a declaration that a converted numeral leaves tied with
those of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
Equality and inequality are not converted so: the declaration of \EXP{=} on
\TYP{Number} is applicable to an integer value and a numeral without coercion,
and so is the top-level declaration of \EXP{\neq}, whose parameters are of type
\TYP{Any}; the compiled type checker selects these and converts neither
operand, and \EXP{=} then compares the two as rationals, through the case for a
numeral that this change adds to \VAR{exactValue}, the function by which
\TYP{Number}'s \EXP{=} takes an exact value.
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} states in its api, for the same reason, the additive and
multiplicative operators its body declares.
\TYP{IntLiteral} declares its own \VAR{zero}, \VAR{one}, \VAR{even},
\VAR{odd}, \VAR{floor}, \VAR{ceiling}, \VAR{truncate}, \OPR{DIVIDES},

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

## The goal

- **The measuring stick.** Finish what the designers intended, judged by the specification in `Specification/`, the Working Draft of 2010-12 as the revival revises it, with the 2012 Types chapter cited beside it; not redesign the language. The measure is one program, microGPT, compiled to bytecode and running fast. A pure-Java microGPT is written later as the floor to measure against. The specification is a living document that reflects the changes we make. The tree is tagged `sealed-tree` at the map's last commit; commits after it edit the original sources, test-driven.
- **How he weighs his calls where the designers left no word.** "I don't care about type theoretical purity and I'm accepting all unfinished corners of the language because I want to get to a compiled version of micro GPT. And I think this is the right pragmatic approach so that we do not get bogged down in weeds. Theory. We want to get this one program running fast. That's our guiding star. But along the way, I want to stay true to the spirit of Fortress." He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and relies on the record: "I assume those people knew much more than I do right now." The check he asked for is a thorough top-tier review of every decision of his against the designers' intent, for errors of commission and of omission (`reviews/decisions-review/evidence.md`, `judgement.md`, `popl-recheck.md`); its items are decisions below.
- **The readable expression.** The toy problem is microGPT and the search is for its most readable expression: "we are searching for the optimal expression of the microGPT algorithm for readability." Fortress's mathematical notation and Iverson's APL notation (with Hsu's data design for data-flow algorithms) are the two sources. The Hsu-style flat program gave "a few lumps of coal", not a diamond; the vocabulary is where any polishing happens. C4 is the APL target form; C2's tuple hyperparameter form is what a strand assignment expands to; the semicolon form is set aside.
- **The APL side quest is closed.** It was a curiosity, then a ladder to learn APL, then native code (not an interpreter in an interpreter) with microGPT as its target; its remaining ground (tacit, characters, nested arrays) is not pursued.
- **The 2D notation is a gimmick.** Fortify's mathematical rendering is "a neat gimmick, not a good idea": it encodes one perspective on a computation into the syntax, while the same mathematics can be written many ways; APL's glyph-per-transformation is the purer realisation. Presentation only, not on the path, not an argument for Fortress; no work on it unless he asks.
- **The type checker on interpreter programs.** He wants the checker, which runs only on the compile path, usable on interpreter programs, and considers it low-hanging fruit. It comes after the switch-over, when walk also takes the static coercions the checker inserts (the entry on walk's choice of coercions).

## History he knows (do not re-explain)

- **The project's end.** DARPA's HPCS did not take Sun into phase three (2006) and the project lived on at Sun Labs until 2012. His reading: they did no work on performance, "mucked around with syntax", and the promise that a sufficiently advanced compiler would later make mathematical types fast was never true; the funding was pulled for good reason.
- **Boxed numerics.** The compiled path is only about ten times the interpreter because numerics are boxed (`FRR64`, no `DADD`); "without unboxed doubles and arrays of doubles, what are we even doing here". The first measurement's scalar loop was an edge case microGPT never hits (literals in the loop, a `:=` accumulator); the fairer test he asked for agreed with him (FACTS § Execution model). The storage is his decision below; unboxed arithmetic is phase 6 of the plan.
- **Hsu's critique** of language paradigms as accidental complexity; he is "coming around to his point of view".
- **The third-party Java 9 port** gets no credit and no mention: "I don't wanna see them mentioned anywhere." CLAUDE.md no longer describes the tree as the port's migration grafted on the history; the other files that repeat that sentence wait for the lineage cleanup (`PLAN.md`). His plan to rename the graft-free `clean-ladder` branch to `main` was not carried out.

1317:The compiled type checker enforces the requirement on a trait with static
No example of this specification changes: \TYP{ExclusiveMolecule}, which
has no static parameters, is still not allowed.
The compiled type checker enforces the requirement on a trait with static
parameters over the declarations it sees: a trait or object declared in
another component, below such a trait and a subtype of no listed type, is
not refused (row~487 of the revival's gap ledger). It compares the declarations it sees by their names: for a parameterized \VAR{T} its verdict can depend on how an extender spells its static parameters, and a trait or object that extends a trait of the same simple name in another API counts as an extender (rows~489 and~490).
The interpreter checks at load the traits and objects that explicitly extend a
trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause declared in the component it executes, and
refuses one that is neither a subtype of a listed type nor another of the
extenders that \secref{trait-decls} allows.
It does not yet check a clause declared in another component, of the program
or of \library\ (rows~22, 487, 551, 595 and~596), an object expression that
extends such a trait (row~597), or that each listed type extends \VAR{T}
(row~598).
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex},
lines 230--241, a draft note:

\EXP{\TYP{ImmutableArray}\llbracket{}T, \mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket} of \library;
and that the compiled path's own library declares no such type.
The normative text is unchanged.

revival's decision of 23~September 2026 that the implementers' later word
outweighs text that the designers left unfinished.
The text and its draft notes name \TYP{HeapSequence} and
\TYP{ReadOnlyHeapSequence} (``We agreed to implement varargs tuples using
\TYP{ReadOnlyHeapSequence} which is immutable and invariant.
We'll add \TYP{MakeReadOnlyHeapSequence} into the core library.''), and no
library declares either.
The authors of the compiled type checker named a type for the parameter,
\EXP{\TYP{ImmutableArray}\llbracket{}T, \mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket}, with the
comment ``Replace ImmutableArray with ImmutableHeapSequence when
ImmutableHeapSequence is put into the libraries''
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/Types.java}, lines
47--49, in the revival's repository), and the interpreter binds the parameter
to an immutable one-dimensional array of the arguments that the factory
\VAR{\_\_immutableFactory1} of \library\ builds
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/NonPrimitive.java},
lines 224--251), a value of that type.
The type is immutable, as the draft note asks.
Before this change the compiled type checker typed the parameter in the body
as \VAR{T}, the type of one argument, and read a parameter list with plain
bindings before a varargs binding as if the varargs binding were one more plain
binding, so that a call that passed no argument, or more than one, for the
varargs binding after plain bindings was refused (row~604 of the revival's gap
ledger).
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-checker-defects/REPORT.md} in the
revival's repository.

parameter to a call as \secref{function-app} and
\secref{applicability-with-special-params} say, whatever the number of
arguments for the varargs binding, none among them, each a subtype of the type
of the binding or convertible to it; and it types the parameter in the body at
\EXP{\TYP{ImmutableArray}\llbracket{}T, \mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket} of \library,
where it typed it as \VAR{T}.
Under the compiled path's own library, which declares no \TYP{ImmutableArray},
it refuses a body that uses a varargs parameter, naming the type.
The code generator does not yet compile a function with a varargs parameter,
so no program with one runs on the compiled path.
The interpreter is unchanged.
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/functions.tex},
lines 178--182, which stand unchanged and are now followed by the box:
\begin{quote}
The type of a varargs parameter
is \EXP{\TYP{HeapSequence}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} where \VAR{T} is
the type mentioned in (or inferred for) that binding.
\note{See the library section for a discussion of
\TYP{HeapSequence}.}
\end{quote}
\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
\end{description}

'''

#!/bin/bash
# Compile-path ladder, restricted to the files this rung can affect.
#
# A copy of ../run-ladder.sh with two changes: the ladder root and output
# directory are private to this worktree, and the two whole-corpus loops are
# replaced by one driven by subset.txt (corpus<TAB>file per line).
#
# Pushes every interpreter test program (ProjectFortress/tests/*.fss) and every
# file in ProjectFortress/not_working_library_tests/ through the compiler path
# unchanged and records how far each one gets.
#
# Reproduce:  bash explorations/compile-ladder/run-ladder.sh
# Outputs:    explorations/compile-ladder/raw/<corpus>/<name>.{compile,run}
#             explorations/compile-ladder/results.tsv
#
# The run uses a private cache tree so it never touches default_repository/caches
# (fortress.caches system property + FORTRESS_CACHES env; ProjectProperties.java:283,
# same mechanism the suite uses at build.xml:941-943), and a private java.io.tmpdir
# so the 5.8 MB Rats! temp directory of every grammar-importing run (RatsUtil.java:138-144)
# is swept per file instead of filling the disk.

set -u

source "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../../../explorations/experiment/env.sh"

LADDER_ROOT="${LADDER_ROOT:-$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp/ladder-r1}"
export LADDER_CACHES="$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-caches"
export LADDER_TMP="$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-tmp"
export FORTRESS_CACHES="$LADDER_CACHES"
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx2g -Xss64m -Dfortress.caches=$LADDER_CACHES -Djava.io.tmpdir=$LADDER_TMP"

PRISTINE="$LADDER_ROOT/pristine"
OUT="$FORTRESS_HOME/explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static"
RAW="$OUT/raw"
TSV="$OUT/results.tsv"

COMPILE_TIMEOUT=120
RUN_TIMEOUT=60
MIN_FREE_KB=512000

mkdir -p "$RAW/tests" "$RAW/not_working_library_tests" "$LADDER_TMP"

disk_guard () {
    local free
    free=$(df -P / | awk 'NR==2{print $4}')
    if [ "$free" -lt "$MIN_FREE_KB" ]; then
        echo "STOP: only ${free} KB free on / (floor ${MIN_FREE_KB} KB)" | tee -a "$OUT/ladder.log"
        exit 2
    fi
    echo "-- disk free ${free} KB, cache $(du -sm "$LADDER_CACHES" | cut -f1) MB"
}

# Step 1: the compiler-world library, in the order repo-internals.md gives.
build_library () {
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1
    local f
    for f in LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss \
             ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss \
             ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss ; do
        echo "library: $f"
not_working_library_tests
tests
2

# Step 2: one known-good compiled program must print PASS before the ladder starts.
sanity () {
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1
    timeout 200 ../bin/fortress compile library_tests/Integer1.fss > /dev/null 2>&1 || return 1
    timeout 60 ../bin/fortress run Integer1 2>&1 | grep -q PASS
}

# Keep only the library's own cache entries; a program's entries are never reused.
prune_cache () {
    ( cd "$LADDER_CACHES" && find . -type f -print ) | sort > "$LADDER_TMP/.now"
    ( cd "$PRISTINE" && find . -type f -print ) | sort > "$LADDER_TMP/.keep"
    comm -23 "$LADDER_TMP/.now" "$LADDER_TMP/.keep" | while read -r p; do
        rm -f "$LADDER_CACHES/$p"
    done
}

component_of () {
    # component/api name as declared, which is what `fortress run` wants
    sed -n 's/^[[:space:]]*\(component\|api\)[[:space:]]\+\([A-Za-z0-9_.]\+\).*/\2/p' "$1" | head -1
}

run_one () {
    local corpus="$1" path="$2"
    local base name comp crc rrc t0 t1 ct rt
    base=$(basename "$path")
    name="${base%.*}"
    comp=$(component_of "$path")
    [ -n "$comp" ] || comp="$name"

    t0=$(date +%s)
    timeout -k 5 "$COMPILE_TIMEOUT" ../bin/fortress compile "$path" \
        > "$RAW/$corpus/$base.compile" 2>&1
    crc=$?
    t1=$(date +%s); ct=$((t1-t0))

    rrc=""
    rt=""
    if [ "$crc" -eq 0 ] && [ "${base##*.}" = "fss" ]; then
        t0=$(date +%s)
        timeout -k 5 "$RUN_TIMEOUT" ../bin/fortress run "$comp" \
            > "$RAW/$corpus/$base.run" 2>&1
        rrc=$?
        t1=$(date +%s); rt=$((t1-t0))
    fi

    printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' \
        "$corpus" "$base" "$comp" "$crc" "$rrc" "$ct" "$rt" >> "$TSV"
    echo "$corpus/$base crc=$crc rrc=$rrc ${ct}s"
}

main () {
    echo "=== ladder start $(date -Is) ==="
    disk_guard
    if [ ! -d "$PRISTINE" ]; then
        build_library
        rm -rf "$PRISTINE"; cp -a "$LADDER_CACHES" "$PRISTINE"
    fi
    sanity || { echo "SANITY FAILED: library_tests/Integer1 did not print PASS"; exit 1; }
    echo "sanity ok: library_tests/Integer1 compiles and prints PASS"
    prune_cache

    : > "$TSV"
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1

    local n=0 line corpus f
    while IFS=$'\t' read -r corpus f; do
        [ -n "$corpus" ] || continue
        run_one "$corpus" "$corpus/$f"
        n=$((n+1))
        rm -rf "${LADDER_TMP:?}"/fortress*rats
        if [ $((n % 10)) -eq 0 ]; then prune_cache; disk_guard; fi
    done < "$OUT/subset.txt"
    prune_cache
    echo "=== ladder done $(date -Is), $n files ==="
    disk_guard
}

#!/bin/bash
# The gate's checker-count stage: run the bytecode compiler's static checker over the
# INTERPRETER's library, with the interpreter's prelude in scope, and print the per-api
# error table, the total and the crash line that follows it.
#
# Why it exists: POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-21, "the library route" - one library, the
# interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks - and step 1 of
# coordinator/library-route-judgement.md, which makes the distance to that goal a
# permanent gate stage rather than a one-off script. A change in the count is reported, not red (checker-gate-review.md).
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched:
# javac output and the checker's caches go to the scratch directory (default: $TMPDIR
# or /tmp), and the caches are given to the JVM as -Dfortress.caches, honoured through
# ProjectProperties.java:261-269,283, so default_repository/ is never read or written.
# Exit 0 if the table was produced, 1 if it could not be. 20 s in the main tree,
# measured 2026-09-22; it needs no library rebuild and no warm cache.

# The two sources beside this script are copies, taken 2026-09-22 from

# to a tracked file) and shadow-src/.../StaticChecker.java, a copy of
# ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java with three
# instrumentation points added: it names each compilation unit it checks and prints that
# unit's error count, and it catches the OverloadingChecker crash instead of dying on it.
# It is put AHEAD of ProjectFortress/build on the classpath, the technique of
